title: Switching identity: su, sudo, and sudoers
lead: Learn when and how to use root privileges: prefer one-command sudo and manage its policy safely with visudo.
objectives: Explain that root has UID 0, the difference between `su -` and `sudo`, and which password each command asks for.
Run one administrative command with `sudo` and inspect your permissions with `sudo -l`.
Open a full root login shell with `sudo -i`, close it with `exit`, and avoid staying root unnecessarily.
Know that `/etc/sudoers` defines privilege policy and must only be edited with `visudo`.

sections.title: Who is root? su and sudo
body: On Linux, **root** is the superuser with UID 0. Root can manage system files and other accounts; a wrong command can cause serious damage. Stay in your normal account for everyday work and use administrator privileges only when needed.

`su - USER` switches to the target account and asks for that account's password. `su -` switches to root, but root password login may be disabled on systems such as Ubuntu. The `-` loads the target user's login environment (for example, `HOME` and profile).

`sudo COMMAND` lets an authorized user authenticate with their own password and run only the specified command as another user, usually root. A sudo rule can also be configured not to ask for a password. Running one command with sudo is safer than keeping a root session open.

sections.title: One command and administrator sessions
body: `sudo whoami` prints `root`; plain `whoami` prints your own account. Sudo elevates only that command, so your shell remains a normal user when the command ends.

`sudo -l` lists the commands your account may run. `sudo -u USER COMMAND` runs one command as a specified user when the policy allows it. The rules depend on the distribution and organization; membership in `wheel` is common on Rocky/Alma and `sudo` on Ubuntu/Debian.

`sudo -i` opens root's login shell; `whoami` then prints root and `HOME` is `/root`. `sudo -s` opens a root shell that keeps more of the current environment. Both are full, high-risk sessions: keep them short and use `exit` to leave. Sudo may cache authentication for a while; `sudo -k` invalidates that cache.

commands.what: Lists the commands and rules available to your account through sudo.
commands.where: Before investigating your permissions or an access error.
commands.why: Shows the machine's actual policy rather than assumptions.

commands.what: Runs one command as the specified user.
commands.where: When checking how a service or job behaves under another account.
commands.why: Tests the target account's permissions without opening a root session.

commands.where: For a brief, controlled session that needs several admin commands.
commands.why: Loads root's HOME and startup environment.

commands.why: Prevents a previous authentication from being reused by subsequent commands.

sections.warn: A forgotten command inside `sudo -i` still runs as root. Prefer `sudo COMMAND` for short tasks; after leaving a root shell, use `whoami` to verify you returned to your normal account.

sections.title: sudoers: manage privilege policy safely
body: `/etc/sudoers` and files in `/etc/sudoers.d/` define who may run which commands as which target users. Never edit these files directly with `nano`, `vim`, or `echo`: a single syntax error can break all sudo access.

Use `sudo visudo` to inspect and edit the policy. To open a separate rule file, use `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/NAME`; `visudo` checks the syntax before saving. For example, `alice ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx` permits only that command.

`NOPASSWD` removes the password prompt, for example `alice ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx`. Use it only when truly needed, with the full command path and a narrow scope. Granting unrestricted access with `ALL` or opening a general-purpose shell without a password is not a safe rule. Check the result with `sudo -l`.

commands.what: Edits sudo policy with locking and syntax validation.
commands.where: When adding or changing a sudoers rule.
commands.why: Reduces the risk of saving a malformed file and breaking sudo access.

commands.what: Safely edits the specified sudoers file.
commands.where: When creating a separate sudoers.d rule supported by the distribution.
commands.why: Keeps rules separate from the main file and validates their syntax.

commands.what: Checks the syntax of sudoers files.
commands.why: Confirms that the file can be read and parsed.

commands.where: When checking whether a policy change applies to a user.
commands.why: Lets you compare the written rule with the effective permissions.

sections.danger: `NOPASSWD: ALL` lets a user run every command without a password. Limit the rule to the required user, exact command path, and necessary arguments; write it with `visudo` and verify it with `sudo -l`.

sections.title: A safe administrator workflow
body: First verify the target and its impact from your normal account; when elevated access is required, run only the necessary command with sudo. If it fails, do not blindly add `sudo`: inspect `id`, `sudo -l`, and the file permissions.

When the work is done, leave any root session with `exit`. Never put passwords in command history, edit sudoers directly, or run an unfamiliar command as root. On a real VM, take a snapshot before changing system policy.

commands.why: Catches a broken rule before it is relied upon.

sections.tip: Apply least privilege: grant no more than the required user, target account, command, and arguments.

vm.intro: This section inspects privilege policy on a real system; it does not change configuration. Take a VM snapshot if possible. Enter your password only at the terminal's sudo prompt.

v01.title: Inspect your normal identity
v01.text: Show your normal account and group memberships with `id`.
differs: User names and UIDs vary by distribution; your own values are expected.
Ubuntu commonly uses the `sudo` group; Rocky/Alma commonly use `wheel`.

v02.title: Use sudo for one command
v02.text: Run `sudo whoami` and verify that the effective user is root.
differs: No characters appear while typing the password; that is expected.
A `not in the sudoers file` error means your account has not been granted permission; ask an administrator.

v03.title: Verify the effective UID
v03.text: Run `sudo id -u` to verify that the privileged command runs with UID 0.
differs: `id -u` prints the effective UID as a number; root's UID is 0.
If the command is denied, inspect permissions with `sudo -l`.

v04.title: Read your sudo permissions
v04.text: List commands permitted for your account with `sudo -l`; do not change any rules.

blocks.expected: User student may run the following commands

differs: The user name and rules vary by distribution.
If the output includes `NOPASSWD`, note which exact command it covers; do not change the rule.

v05.title: Check sudoers syntax
v05.text: Run `sudo visudo -c` to verify that the current sudo configuration parses. This command does not edit the files.
differs: A distribution may also check included files; expect a `parsed OK`-style line for each file.
If an error appears, do not edit the file directly; report it to the system administrator.

q1.q: What is the main difference between `sudo COMMAND` and `su -`?
options: Both always require the root password
`sudo` runs one permitted command; `su -` opens the target account's login session
`sudo` permanently turns the user into root
q1.explain: `sudo` grants privilege for a command; `su -` switches to another account's login shell.

q2.q: Why use `visudo` to edit the sudo policy file?
options: It checks syntax and reduces the chance of saving a broken rule
It adds all users to the sudo group
q2.explain: `visudo` locks the file while editing and checks its syntax before saving.

q3.q: Which sudo rule follows least privilege?
options: Grant one user only the exact command they need
Share the root password with the team
Run every command in a permanent root shell
q3.explain: Limit access to the right user and required command; avoid broad `ALL` rules.

q4.q: If `su -` rejects the root password on Ubuntu, what is a likely explanation?
options: The terminal does not support root sessions
The root account may be locked for password login; an authorized user should use `sudo`
q4.explain: Ubuntu installations often lock the root account; an authorized user uses sudo for administration.

summary: Root has UID 0. `su -` opens the target account's login session; `sudo COMMAND` runs one permitted command with elevated privileges.
`sudo -l` shows actual permissions; `sudo -i` opens a full root login shell and should be closed with `exit` when finished.
Edit sudoers policy only with `visudo` and validate its syntax with `visudo -c`.
Keep `NOPASSWD` and especially `ALL` rules narrow; grant only the required user, command, and arguments.

glossary.meaning: The account with UID 0 and system-wide administrative privileges.
A tool that lets an authorized user run a specific command as another user.
A tool for switching the current session to another user account.
The policy defining sudo permissions by user, target account, and command.
A tool that edits sudoers files with locking and syntax validation.
A sudo rule option that removes the password prompt for specified commands.
